games.chapterTitle: All-Russian Amateur Tournament at St. Petersburg, February, 1909
games.overallPlan: White turns Black's premature 5...Nd4 and 14...Kd7 into a fierce central and queenside-cum-kingside onslaught, sacrificing an exchange via 17. exf5! to deflect Black's light-squared bishop and force the queen into a7 with a decisive bind.

diagrams.printerErratum: Diagram after 20...c5 still prints Black's c-pawn on c6 (19...c6) while showing 20. Qxa7 already played (corrected c-pawn position is on c5).

annotations.summary: After 3. Bc4, Black's cleanest equalizing continuation is the central fork trick 3...Nxe4! (cross-referenced to Game 41).
Sending the knight to d4 is premature because it loses time and ends up shutting in Black's light-squared bishop; breaking the pin first with 5...h6 keeps equality.

variations.summary: Equalizing line for Black instead of 5...Nd4.

annotations.summary: Forces the exchange on c3 immediately: retreating 6...Ba5 allows White to gain queenside space with 7. b4 followed by Nd5, while 6. f4 d6 7. Nf3 was an alternative.

variations.summary: Viable alternative setup for White.

annotations.summary: Prevents Black's centralizing ...d5 break with tempo/comfort; playing 8. Bd2 first allows 8...d5! 9. exd5 Nxd5 10. Qe2 f6, whereas after 8. h4 h6 9. Bd2, ...d5 leaves White on top.

variations.summary: Black achieves active central counterplay if White omits 8. h4.
White keeps the advantage once h4 and ...h6 are included.

annotations.summary: Capturing 8...Nxg5 walks into 9. hxg5 Ng8 10. g6! smashing the kingside.
Launching a kingside g-pawn push is somewhat superficial; simple development with 10. Nge2 followed by Ng3 gave a clean positional edge without complications.
Black misses the energetic defense 12...hxg5 13. hxg5 Rxh1 14. Qxh1 Ng8 15. Qh7 O-O-O! which trades off the inactive h8 rook and yields good counter-chances.

variations.summary: Active defence exchanging the h8 rook.

subvariations.summary: After 14. gxf6, Black captures on g1 with check and seizes a winning advantage.

annotations.summary: Leaving the king in the center invites a decisive attack; Black should have opened the h-file and castled queenside with 14...hxg5 15. hxg5 O-O-O 16. Qe3 Kb8 17. Rg1.

variations.summary: Safeguards Black's king on the queenside.

annotations.summary: Prepares to centralize the h3 knight via f4 after f4 and ...f5.
If 16...h5, White still crashes through with 17. Qg3 exf4 18. Nxf4 Nxf4 19. Bxf4 Bxe4 20. O-O-O!.

variations.summary: Winning attack for White if Black tries 16...h5.

annotations.summary: Decisive exchange sacrifice: White deflects Black's light-squared bishop away from defense so the pawn advances d4-d5 can expose b7.
Keeping the king on e8 fails cleanly to 19. Qg1 d5 20. Bb5+ Kd8 21. Bd7.

variations.summary: Refutation of 18...Ke8 (and 18...Kd8 19. Qg1 threatening mate).

subvariations.summary: Immediate loss of the c6 pawn and queen/king collapse.

annotations.summary: Clever defense: if White greedily takes the h1 bishop (20. Qxh1), 20...d5 21. Bb3 Qxe6 seizes the initiative.
White's 20. Qxa7! hits b7; Black advances ...c5 to contest the center before 21. d4!.
Justifies the 17. exf5 sacrifice: 21...exd4 fails immediately to 22. cxd4 cxd4 23. Ba5! forcing mate.
Black cannot stop 23. Rxb7: both 22...Qb8 23. Qa4 Rd8 and 22...Qc7 23. Rb5! lead to irresistible mating threats.

variations.summary: Forced mate after 22...Qb8.

subvariations.summary: If 23...Qc7 instead of 23...Rd8, White forces the win with 24. Rb5! followed by 25. Ra5.

annotations.summary: Wins another pawn while holding Black's bishop in a fatal pin via the threat of Ba5 and mate.
Forces ...Rxf5, after which Black drops a full piece on e7 to White's passed e6-e7 pawn and Queen checks.

games.chapterTitle: All-Russian Amateur Tournament at St. Petersburg, February, 1909
games.overallPlan: In the Exchange Ruy Lopez endgame, Black plays 9...c4! to seize dark squares with his bishop pair, sacrifices a pawn temporarily to immobilize White's kingside, and uses central rook/knight coordination to launch a mating attack.

annotations.summary: Lasker played 9. b3 against Tarrasch (1908), who erred by allowing bishop trades with 9...Bc6; Alekhine considers 9...c4! a positional refutation.

variations.summary: Tarrasch's passive setup in 1908 allowing an exchange of his dark-squared bishop.

annotations.summary: Sacrifices a pawn to fracture White's queenside pawns and seize permanent initiative with the two bishops.
Other 12th moves also leave Black better: 12. Nd4 c5 13. Nb3 Re8 or 12. O-O Bc2 13. Nd2 Nf6 14. Ng3 Bc5 recover the pawn with superior piece play.

variations.summary: Black builds strong pressure on e4 and the dark squares.
Black regains the pawn cleanly with active pieces.

annotations.summary: Prevents 14. Nd4 (which would drop material to 14...Rxd4) and ties White down to defending the f2-a7 diagonal.
White's plan to blockade c5 fails; 15. Nd4 Bxd4 16. cxd4 Rxd4 17. Bb2 Rd3 offered slightly better drawing chances despite Black's d-file pressure.

variations.summary: Best practical resistance for White.

annotations.summary: White could resist longer with 19. Bb4 Rd1+ 20. Rxd1 Rxd1+ 21. Kf2 Nd7 22. Nfg3 Rxe1 23. Nxe1 Nxc5, though Black still wins easily with two bishops and a passed pawn.

variations.summary: Endgame line after trading rooks.

annotations.summary: Sacrifices the knight tactically because 21. Nxc2 loses to a five-move mating attack starting with 21...Nxe4+ (double check).

variations.summary: Forced mate in 5 if White captures the c2 bishop.

annotations.summary: Wins the c3 pawn cleanly, as 22. Rhc1 drops a piece to 22...Rxd4 followed by ...Nd3+.
Exchange sacrifice exposing White's king and winning quickly; trading rooks via 25. Rhd1 fails similarly.

variations.summary: Simple won rook ending if White chooses 25. Rhd1.

games.overallPlan: White loses time with 6. Qf3 and castles queenside into a ready-made Black pawn storm; Black locks in the bishop pair vs bad bishop, trades queens into a superior endgame, and breaks through with ...d4! and rook penetration.

annotations.summary: Better than its early reputation: helps simplify after 4. exd5 and leaves Black well placed against 4. e5 c5.
Avoids the tactical traps of 4...dxe4 5. Qg4! where White gains strong attacking play against g7 and d5.

variations.summary: Dangerous gambit attack for White if Black plays 4...dxe4 5...Nf6.
Also grants White a strong initiative.

annotations.summary: Misplaces the queen and leads to awkward minor-piece coordination; 6. Bd3 followed by Nge2 and O-O was sounder.
Strategic error: White lacks kingside compensation for Black's natural queenside attack; 9. Rc1 followed by O-O was preferable.
Eliminates White's light-squared bishop so a Black knight can establish an outpost on c4.
Small tactical slip allowing White to liquidate queens; Black already stood strategically winning and could press directly with ...a5 and ...b5-b4.
If 18...Qd7, White starts kingside counterplay with 19. h4 and Rh3.
Sets up ...c4 and ...d4; playing 22...b4 straight away allows 23. axb4 cxb4 24. Bd4.
Decisive breakthrough giving Black a dangerous passed c-pawn; if White tries 24. Bb2 instead of taking, 24...Nb6 followed by ...a4 dominates.
White cannot afford to exchange both rooks via 27. Rd1 Rxd1+ because Black wins the pawn endgame easily with ...g5, ...h6-h5, and ...b4.

variations.summary: Lost king-and-pawn ending for White after trading all rooks (Black plays ...Kf8-e7-e6 and wins the e5 pawn).

annotations.summary: Black's rook dominates the second rank, reducing the rest of the game to straightforward endgame technique.

games.overallPlan: Against 7...b6 in the Queen's Gambit Declined, White castles queenside after 10. h4!, uses 20. Ne6! and 22. Rxg6! to win a pawn in transition to a rook ending, and decides the pawn race with the subtle waiting king move 44. Ke2!.

annotations.summary: After 7...c5, White should play 8. Rd1 (transposing into Capablanca-Lasker match structures) rather than automatic queenside castling.
Once Black puts the pawn on b6, blocking c5/b6 squares for his queen and knight, White's O-O-O plan gains real attacking punch.
Stops 10...Ne4 before White castles queenside.
Targets the isolated d5 pawn; against 12...Ne4 13. Bxe7 Nxc3+ 14. Qxc3 Qxe7 15. Kb1, White prepares Rc1 and Rhd1.

variations.summary: Positional pressure against d5 and on the c-file.

annotations.summary: Passive preparation for ...Bf8; Black needed immediate queenside expansion with ...a6 and ...b5.
Insufficient due to the hidden 22. Rxg6! sacrifice; yet even after 14...Nf8 15. Rhg1 b5 16. Nf5 White keeps a clear advantage.

variations.summary: White maintains a strong kingside initiative.

annotations.summary: Initiates a tactical sequence that wins a clean pawn and reaches a won rook endgame.
Compulsory: 21...g6 collapses immediately to 22. Rxh7! Qxe6 23. Qh4 Qe4+ 24. Qxe4 Rxe4 25. Rdh1.

variations.summary: Winning attack on the open h-file if Black plays 21...g6.

annotations.summary: Avoids an immediate queen swap that would leave Black's rook ideally placed on e6; forces ...Rxe5 instead.
Forced: 29...Re6 allows 30. Rxe6 followed by Rh7+.
Calculated liquidation into a king-and-pawn ending: 42. Kd4 loses to ...Ke6 and 42. Kb4 draws in a mutual pawn race, so White uses a subtle king triangulation.

variations.summary: Mutual pawn race yields only a draw if White grabs on b5.

annotations.summary: Key zugzwang/timing move forcing ...Ke6, after which 45. Kf2! (not 45. Kc3? Kxe5) secures the winning break and opposition.

games.overallPlan: After 6. Bxc6 bxc6, Black overreaches with 7...Qe8 and 8...Nxe4, allowing 9. Nh6+! and 10. Re1; White wins a pawn cleanly with 16. Rb1!, establishes a winning kingside pawn majority, and finishes with a back-rank mating net.

annotations.summary: 6...dxc6 is stronger, leaving Black the bishop pair and queen-file counterplay against either 7. Nxe5 or 7. d3.
More solid is 7...Re8 8. d4 Bxc3 9. bxc3 Nxe4 10. Qf3 with only a slight edge for White.
Leads to trouble after 9. Nh6+!; Black could equalize by trading knights 8...Nxg4 9. Qxg4 d5.

variations.summary: Equalizing simplification instead of 8...Nxe4.

annotations.summary: Seizes the initiative; accepting the knight via 9...gxh6 10. Qg4+ Kh8 11. Qxe4 also leaves White clearly better.

variations.summary: Clean advantage for White if Black takes the knight.

annotations.summary: Underestimates 16. Rb1!; 11...Nxc3 12. bxc3 Be7 13. Qh5 Be6 14. f4 offered a tougher defense.
15. Rb1 Qe6 16. Rxb2 bxc3 17. Rb3 was also winning, but Alekhine prefers 15. Nxf7+ to keep Black from attacking on an open g-file.
Secures a winning extra pawn with a healthy kingside majority while Black's queenside doubled pawns are crippled; 16...bxa1=Q runs into 17. Nxe5 Qf4 18. Nd3.
Swapping queens via 20...Qxe3 loses effortlessly to White's central rook control and passed kingside advance.

variations.summary: Textbook winning endgame plan for White (followed by Ke1, Ra3-c3-c5, and c4).

annotations.summary: The queen's infiltration decides rapidly; after 31...Bf1 32. Ra5 Qd1 33. Kh2 Bxh2 34. Kxh2, 34...Qf3+ fails to finish and White forces mate with 36. Rh8!.

games.overallPlan: Facing an inverted Ruy Lopez, Black gives up a pawn temporarily with 19...Ne5! to neutralize White's bishops, regains the initiative by sacrificing the e-pawn via 31...b4!, and coordinates queen and knight against White's overextended kingside pawns.

annotations.summary: Lets White undouble pawns too easily; 7...O-O 8. O-O d6 was steadier.
Forced because 9...Rd8 fails to 10. Nxd5! Qe5 11. c4 c6 12. Bf4 Qe6 13. Bg4! f5 14. Bxf5 winning the queen.
Allows Black's knight to reach a better square; 15. Bb3 Na6 16. Rad1 Qc7 17. Qh5 kept White's edge.
Overambitious; White could equalize safely via 17. g4 Bg6 18. Nxg6 hxg6 19. Bxb5 Rxb5 20. Bg5 Rxg5 21. Rxe8+.
Tactically sound counterstroke leaving d6 en prise because 20. Qxd6 Nxf3+ 21. Kf2 Qxd6 22. Rxd6 Nxe1 23. Rd2! g6 24. Re2 Rxe3 25. Kxe3 Re8+ 26. Kd2 Nf3+ 27. Kc3 Rxe2 28. Nxe2 c5 favors Black.

variations.summary: Tactical refutation if White captures the d6 knight.

annotations.summary: Energetic bid for counterplay and drawing chances; 28. Rxe4 Rxe4 29. Rxe4 Qa1 30. Re1 Qc3 leaves Black clearly ahead.
Marks the final attack: sacrificing the e4 pawn lets Black's queen and knight infiltrate fatally against White's weakened kingside.
41...h5! was even faster, exploiting the open f-file and dark squares via 42. Qc3 Rxf5+ 43. gxf5 Qxf5+ 44. Kg2 Qxe4+ 45. Kxh3 Qg4#.

variations.summary: Immediate decisive attack with 41...h5!.

annotations.summary: 48...Rd6+ forces the trade of rooks into an effortlessly winning knight-vs-bishop endgame.

games.overallPlan: White exploits the dark-square weakness created by 4...g6 with 7. Ndb5! and 8. f4, and crashes through with the temporary two-piece sacrifice 13. b4! followed by the decisive pin 17. Rb1!.

annotations.summary: 2...d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. d4 Nf6 leads cleanly to a solid French structure; after 2...c5, White can also play 3. Nf3 Nc6 4. d4.
Weakens d6 and the dark squares; 4...Nd4 (as in Alekhine-Leonhardt) equalizes cleanly.
Exposes the dark-square hole on d6, forcing Black's bishop to lose time with 7...Be5.
Invites sharp complications rather than allowing 9. c5 after a bishop retreat.
Temporary two-piece sacrifice for a rook that opens the b-file so the White queen penetrates via 17. Rb1!.
Decisive pin: queen retreats such as 17...Qc4 18. Rc1, 17...Qc5 18. Qa4, or 17...Qa5 18. Bd2 all lose.
Prevents 18...Ne7 (which drops the queen to 19. Qxb6 axb6 20. Rxb6 Bxe2 21. Rb8+).

games.overallPlan: Playing a Reversed Sicilian with an extra tempo, White punishes 6...f6 with 8. d4! and 9. Nb5!, dominates the center, prevents ...Nb6 counterplay, and pushes e5-e6-e7 while the Black king is caught on f8.

annotations.summary: Weakens the dark squares and c8 bishop; 6...Nc6 is the natural developing move.
Immediately exploits 6...f6 to blast open the center before Black can consolidate.
Neither alternative helps: 11...Bxd4 12. Qxd4 O-O 13. Rd1 leaves White's g2 bishop dominant, while 11...Bf7 forfeits castling.
Forces 12...Kf8 because 12...c6 allows 13. Nxc6 and 12...Qd7 trades queens into an awful endgame after 13. Qxd7+ Kxd7 14. Rd1.
White could keep both bishops with 18. b3 c4 19. bxc4 Nxc4 20. Rc3 Rc8, though the game continuation avoids giving Black tactical counter-chances.
Launches the decisive central breakthrough.
After 21...fxe5 22. Rxe5, White's initiative is overwhelming; 21...Rhe8 gave the king slightly more shelter.
Essential finesse before fxe5: prevents 25...Bg6.
Overwhelms Black's position; defensive attempts like 26...Bg6 fail to 27. Rxb6! axb6 28. Qxb6.

games.overallPlan: Against the Hanham Philidor, White prevents ...b5 with 8. a4!, builds full kingside pressure (Qe2, Bb3, Rae1, Nh2, f4, Qg4!), penetrates with f5 and Ng6, and converts the resulting exchange-up attack.

annotations.summary: Castling gives Black too cramped a position without counterplay; delaying castling via 6...h6, ...c6, ...Qc7, ...Nf8, ...g5 and ...Ng6 fits the spirit of the Philidor better.
Halts Black's queenside ...b5 expansion permanently.
Preserves the bishop against ...Nxe4 followed by ...d5; 9. Ba2 was even more accurate.
Unsound kingside rook-lift plan (...Kh7, ...g6, ...Kg7); queenside development (...b6, ...Bb7, ...Rad8) with central ...c5 was sounder.
More energetic than 15. f5 (15...exd4 16. Bxd4 Ne5), forcing Black to surrender the g6 square to avoid instant collapse.
Reroutes the knight to g6 to decide the attack.
Black must sacrifice the exchange because allowing 27. Rf4 followed by Rxh6+ would force mate.

games.overallPlan: White's unsound gambit 5. e5 is declined via 5...Qe7, leading into sharp tactics where White deflects Black's forces with 12. Nf3!! and 25. f5!! to enter a winning two-knights-vs-rook endgame converted after reciprocal endgame errors.

diagrams.printerErratum: Diagram on p. 27 prints Black's second rook on e6 (leaving e8 empty) and shows a position inconsistent with 22...KR-K1 (Rfe8), 25...RxBP, 26. Nde6, 27. Rd8+, 30. Rxg8+, 31. Rd8+ Be8, and 35. RxR PxR in the 1927/1965 edition.

errata.note: In Game 10 (Alekhine-Cohn, Stockholm 1912), moves 1-24 validate cleanly to 24. c4 Rxb3, and the concluding endgame from Diagram 4 (p. 28, move 41) through 57. Nb5 validates cleanly; however, the printed text and Diagram 3 across moves 22-40 contain internal contradictions (e6 rook vs 22...Rfe8 and 26. Nde6, e8 empty required for 27. Rd8+ / 30. Rxg8+ / 31. Rd8+ Be8, 25...RxBP vs 25. c5, and b3 white pawn / e5 black pawn at move 40). Per project rules, no unverified middle moves are fabricated.

annotations.summary: Dubious gambit innovation: Black can simply play 5...Nxe5 6. Qe2 Qe7 7. Nf5 Qe6 8. Nd4 Qe7 with an easy draw or try 7...Qb4+ 8. Nc3 d6 for a win.

variations.summary: Black forces a repetition or fights for an advantage.

annotations.summary: Neutralizes Black's kingside attack: 12...Bc5+ 13. Kh1 Nf2+ 14. Rxf2 Qxf2 15. Ne4 wins Black's trapped queen.

variations.summary: Wins the Black queen.

annotations.summary: Protects e5 while blocking Black's ...Rd8.
Dominates Black's minor pieces and guards c2; 21...c5 allows 22. Nc6 winning queenside space.

In the complicated phase around moves 25-35 (see game errata on the 1927 printed score between moves 22 and 40), White launches tactical play leading into an endgame with two knights and a passed c-pawn against a rook, winning cleanly from the Diagram 4 position (p. 28) after 47...Kc6? (instead of 47...Kc4! stopping the pawns).

variations.label: 41.Ncd2 ... 57.Nb5 (from Diagram 4, p. 28)
variations.summary: Validated concluding endgame from p. 28 Diagram 4 (move 41) through resignation at 57. Nb5.

subvariations.summary: If 47...Kc4! instead of 47...Kc6?, Black halts the passed c-pawn and retains winning material.
